items.title: Quincy Jones — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Jerry Hey has worked with me for 35 years.

ctx.x: Yeah, and the rest of them were from I.U.
Indiana. Jerry Hey has worked with me for 35 years. He’s one of the best musicians in the world.
I see his copying – I mean, I see his hand on things you have him do, where you – like the thing with – what is it? – Al Jarreau? What is that wonderful piece? I can’t remember what it was, but . . .

items.title: Jerry Hey interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 2, 2023
items.q: Quincy would call me to do the arranging, he wouldn’t call me to do the playing, but because I was arranging I was playing.

ctx.x: Yeah. Do you miss it that much?

Oh God, terribly. If I could play and not arrange I would take playing. But the playing of the arranging got us in as a section more than my playing did. So you know that’s, the good news is that I can do this arranging and Quincy would call me to do the arranging, he wouldn’t call me to do the playing, but because I was arranging I was playing. And then he found out that we could play but you know, so the arranging kind of got my foot more in the door than the playing I think. So it’s, you know, it’s kind of a…

Do you ever get over the moment of, I don’t know if anxiety is the right word, but the first time you’re reading down what you arranged and you’re in the studio and the producer is there and you’re waiting to hear the comment about your parts — or do they already know sort of what it’s going to sound like?
